strengths: Introduces a unifying conceptual lens—the effective noise scale—that connects several previously separately-studied optimizer/data hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, augmentation) to model merging compatibility, which is a novel angle beyond prior work linking noise only to single-model flatness/generalization.

Very broad empirical validation: multiple architectures (MLP, ResNet, DenseNet, Transformer/GPT, CLIP ViT, ConvNext), multiple datasets/tasks (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45, TinyStories), and multiple merging paradigms (linear interpolation and task arithmetic), plus transfer learning settings, lending reasonably good external validity to the qualitative trend.

The identification of a non-monotonic 'sweet spot' in noise scale for merging effectiveness is an interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive finding, with reasonable supporting evidence (Figure 1, Figures 15-16 showing failure at extremes).

Good use of appendix materials providing extensive additional plots (per-dataset breakdowns, loss landscape slices, Hessian sharpness, hill-to-valley transition analysis) that support the narrative and improve reproducibility/transparency.
Practical relevance: findings could inform practitioners on how to tune training recipes to improve downstream mergeability, an actionable and underexplored question.
weaknesses: The 'unifying' claim for the effective noise scale is only explicitly demonstrated via reparameterization in one controlled experiment (Figure 1, learning rate x batch size on CIFAR100/ResNet18); the individual factor ablations (Sections 3.2-3.4) do not re-derive or verify the unified S̃ curve, so the paper mostly shows that each factor individually exhibits a qualitatively similar (not quantitatively unified) trend rather than rigorously validating one scalar quantity across all axes simultaneously (e.g., weight decay, augmentation).

No new theory is developed; the effective noise scale formula is adopted from prior SDE-based analyses (Mandt et al., Smith et al., McCandlish et al.) without new derivations specific to the merging/global landscape setting, making the core theoretical contribution thin relative to the empirical claims.

The explanation for weight decay's effect relies on the 'effective learning rate' argument, which is only shown to hold for scale-invariant architectures; the negative result for MLP/SVHN, while acknowledged, somewhat weakens the generality of the unifying framework as a single scalar across all architectures.

Much of the evidence is correlational: the paper documents that noise-related hyperparameters correlate with merging gains, but does not fully disentangle confounds such as different single-model capacity/feature-learning trajectories, or possible implicit changes in effective batch statistics, weakening claims of a causal, mechanistic link.

Task arithmetic experiments (Section 4) are less systematic than the linear interpolation experiments—fewer datasets, less rigorous connection back to the effective noise scale metric, and the results (e.g., initialization-dependent dichotomy) are presented more anecdotally without a unifying quantitative story.

No experiments at a scale resembling state-of-the-art LLMs/vision foundation models used in real merging applications (largest model is a 2-layer GPT and CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuning); the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, which limits significance for practitioners merging large modern models.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: most conclusions rest on violin/scatter plots without explicit significance testing across seeds, and 'sweet spot' locations are not consistently characterized quantitatively across settings (e.g., no attempt to predict the optimal noise scale value a priori).

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored question: why do optimization dynamics determine whether independently trained models can be successfully merged, going beyond prior work that only links noise to single-model flatness/generalization.

Very extensive empirical evaluation across many axes: architectures (MLP, ResNet18, DenseNet121, ViT, ConvNext, GPT-2/Transformer), datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, TinyStories, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45), merging methods (linear interpolation, task arithmetic, TIES, SWA), and optimizer components (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, momentum, augmentation, optimizer choice, scheduler).

The 'effective noise scale' offers an intuitive unifying lens that consolidates several previously disparate observations (large LR, small batch, momentum, weight decay via effective LR) into one quantity, and the paper demonstrates a consistent non-monotonic relationship with merging gain across settings.

Goes beyond simple accuracy-gain plots to connect findings to mechanistic explanations: permutation symmetry/rebasin ease, feature (CKA) alignment/diversity, Hessian-based sharpness, and 2D loss-landscape slices, adding some depth to the causal story.
Very thorough appendix with many additional experiments (schedulers, optimizers, transfer settings, TIES with 3 tasks, SWA interactions) that substantially strengthen robustness of the core claims.
Practical implication is useful and actionable: practitioners could potentially reduce hyperparameter search dimensionality by focusing on effective noise level rather than each component separately.
weaknesses: The work is purely empirical/correlational; no theoretical derivation or model explains why the noise-mergeability curve is non-monotonic or predicts the location of the 'critical point,' which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which limits the depth and generality of the contribution.

The effective noise scale S̃ is a heuristic proxy (assuming tr Σ_A constant across runs) rather than a rigorously validated unifying quantity; the paper mostly shows qualitative alignment of curves (Figure 1) rather than quantitative goodness-of-fit or predictive power across settings.

The task-arithmetic results (Section 4) show a clear dichotomy — larger LR helps mergeability under transfer-learning initialization but hurts it under non-transfer initialization — which complicates and partially undercuts the paper's central unifying narrative that noise straightforwardly governs merging success.

Models studied are relatively small-scale (ResNet18/DenseNet121, 2-layer GPT, ViT-B/16 CLIP), and the paper explicitly states no large-scale experiments were run, despite motivating the problem with references to frontier-scale merging (e.g., Command A); it remains unclear how well the findings transfer to modern LLM/large-scale merging pipelines.

Merging-effectiveness metrics vary across sections (accuracy gain, loss gain, normalized accuracy), and it is not always clear how comparable conclusions are across these different measures, or how sensitive results are to the specific bifurcation/decay training protocol (WSD checkpoints) used throughout.

Statistical reporting is somewhat inconsistent — while violin plots suggest many points, it is unclear how many are truly independent training runs versus checkpoints from a shared stable-phase trajectory (partially correlated samples), and formal significance testing or confidence intervals for the core claims (e.g., critical point location) are largely absent.

The core individual findings (large LR/small batch/high momentum yields flatter minima and links to generalization) are largely consistent with well-established prior literature; the main novel contribution is the merging-specific reframing and the noise-scale unification, which, while useful, is somewhat incremental in conceptual novelty.
